A second investigator, starting fresh with the same tools, tested the kind of each fault in your draft answer. Their findings:

### `ts-route-service`: you said `database_call_slow`. They conclude `network_loss` (confidence: medium).
Scope: Affected: the ts-route-service's own DB connection. Its Client DB calls (SELECT ts.route, SELECT ts.route_distances, SELECT ts.route_stations) and its Transaction.commit waits grow with a tail in ~200 ms steps, which pushes its Server spans (queryById, queryAll, queryByIds, queryByStartAndTerminal) to seconds. Not affected: other services' statements to the same database (ts.config, ts.station, ts.train_type, ts.trip, ts.user, ts.orders, ts.price_config) stay at their normal percentiles; the route-service's CPU and memory are flat or lower; its HTTP hops to callers add only ~1 ms; its container metrics keep arriving (no pod loss).
Ruled out:
- `database_call_slow`: The slowdown is not on particular statements with a steady added cost. Commit, which has no SQL child spans, slows too, and the three SELECT types all show a tail in 200 ms steps (p75 ~205 ms, p95 420-600 ms, with p25 moving 0.1 -> 1.6-1.9 ms). Other services' statements to the same database stay at normal percentiles, so the database is not the slow part; the route-service's own connection is.
- `network_delay`: Delay would move the 25th, 50th and 95th percentiles together by hundreds of ms and fail nothing. Here the median stays near normal on most calls (SELECT ts.route_distances p50 0.10 -> 4.52 ms, p25 0.10 -> 1.91 ms) and the extra time is a tail in steps near 200 ms (histogram buckets 200, 400, 600, 800, 1450, 1650, 3100 ms), the TCP retransmission-timeout signature.
- `http_slow`: Caller-to-callee gap is ~1 ms: ts-basic-service POST Client 215.9 ms vs ts-route-service Server 214.9 ms. The HTTP exchange is not held back; the time is inside the route-service around its DB calls.
- `application_method_slow`: The time is spent in Transaction.commit and in the DB-driver Client spans beneath RouteRepository.findById, not in the route's own methods; Session.find route.entity.Route self-time is 0.4 ms and the commit has no child spans, so the wait is on the wire, not in a method body.
- `container_cpu_saturated`: Container CPU usage fell from 0.057 cores (normal) to 0.013 (incident); the pod's CPU limit utilization fell from 0.011 to 0.002. The route-service is idle while its requests wait.
- `process_cpu_saturated`: The route-service's process CPU (k8s.pod.cpu.usage) also fell, 0.057 -> 0.011, so no process saturates its share.
- `container_memory_saturated`: Container memory usage is flat: mean 575.6 MB normal vs 577.1 MB incident, and memory_limit_utilization is 0.187 in both periods.
- `jvm_heap_exhausted`: No JVM heap metrics were available in this case's tables for the route-service, and container memory is flat; there is no sign of heap pressure, so heap exhaustion is not supported.
- `jvm_gc_thrashing`: No JVM GC metrics were recorded for this case, and container memory and CPU are both flat or lower; nothing points to GC pauses.
- `pod_failure`: The route-service's container metrics keep arriving in the incident (53 rows versus 60 normal), its spans and logs continue at lower volume, and no restart appears in the metrics queried; no gap and recovery sequence is visible.
- `pod_unavailable`: The route-service keeps emitting spans (413 per minute) and metric rows (254 per minute) during the incident, so it is not gone.
- `dns_lookup_failed`: No name-resolution errors appear in the route-service's 6 incident ERROR logs or the Client spans; the DB calls complete with latency, not with unknown-host failures. I did not read the text of those 6 ERROR logs, so this rests on the span data.
- `network_corrupt`: Not fully excluded: corruption and loss produce the same 200 ms-step tail. I did not read the 6 route-service ERROR log texts for deserialization or checksum errors, so this is not ruled out by evidence.

Its Client DB calls (SELECT ts.route, SELECT ts.route_distances, SELECT ts.route_stations) and its Transaction.commit waits grow with a tail in ~200 ms steps, which pushes its Server spans (queryById, queryAll, queryByIds, queryByStartAndTerminal) to seconds. Not affected: other services' statements to the same database (ts.config, ts.station, ts.train_type, ts.trip, ts.user, ts.orders, ts.price_config) stay at their normal percentiles; the route-service's CPU and memory are flat or lower; its HTTP hops to callers add only ~1 ms; its container metrics keep arriving (no pod loss).

ruled_out.why: The slowdown is not on particular statements with a steady added cost. Commit, which has no SQL child spans, slows too, and the three SELECT types all show a tail in 200 ms steps (p75 ~205 ms, p95 420-600 ms, with p25 moving 0.1 -> 1.6-1.9 ms). Other services' statements to the same database stay at normal percentiles, so the database is not the slow part; the route-service's own connection is.

Delay would move the 25th, 50th and 95th percentiles together by hundreds of ms and fail nothing. Here the median stays near normal on most calls (SELECT ts.route_distances p50 0.10 -> 4.52 ms, p25 0.10 -> 1.91 ms) and the extra time is a tail in steps near 200 ms (histogram buckets 200, 400, 600, 800, 1450, 1650, 3100 ms), the TCP retransmission-timeout signature.
Caller-to-callee gap is ~1 ms: ts-basic-service POST Client 215.9 ms vs ts-route-service Server 214.9 ms. The HTTP exchange is not held back; the time is inside the route-service around its DB calls.

The time is spent in Transaction.commit and in the DB-driver Client spans beneath RouteRepository.findById, not in the route's own methods; Session.find route.entity.Route self-time is 0.4 ms and the commit has no child spans, so the wait is on the wire, not in a method body.
Container CPU usage fell from 0.057 cores (normal) to 0.013 (incident); the pod's CPU limit utilization fell from 0.011 to 0.002. The route-service is idle while its requests wait.
The route-service's process CPU (k8s.pod.cpu.usage) also fell, 0.057 -> 0.011, so no process saturates its share.
Container memory usage is flat: mean 575.6 MB normal vs 577.1 MB incident, and memory_limit_utilization is 0.187 in both periods.
No JVM heap metrics were available in this case's tables for the route-service, and container memory is flat; there is no sign of heap pressure, so heap exhaustion is not supported.
No JVM GC metrics were recorded for this case, and container memory and CPU are both flat or lower; nothing points to GC pauses.

The route-service's container metrics keep arriving in the incident (53 rows versus 60 normal), its spans and logs continue at lower volume, and no restart appears in the metrics queried; no gap and recovery sequence is visible.
The route-service keeps emitting spans (413 per minute) and metric rows (254 per minute) during the incident, so it is not gone.

No name-resolution errors appear in the route-service's 6 incident ERROR logs or the Client spans; the DB calls complete with latency, not with unknown-host failures. I did not read the text of those 6 ERROR logs, so this rests on the span data.

Not fully excluded: corruption and loss produce the same 200 ms-step tail. I did not read the 6 route-service ERROR log texts for deserialization or checksum errors, so this is not ruled out by evidence.

**Verdict: the evidence does not support `database_call_slow`.** The route-service's slow DB calls look like a network fault on its connection to the database, most likely `network_loss` (scored the same as `network_partition`). Confidence is medium. The lead's `database_call_slow` reading comes from the span totals, not the shape of the calls.

**What the lead's evidence shows, and what it misses**

- **The slowdown is on every DB call from the route-service, not on particular statements.** In the incident, `SELECT ts.route`, `SELECT ts.route_distances`, `SELECT ts.route_stations` and `Transaction.commit` all slow down. Commit has no child spans, so its time is the wire round-trip to the database, not statement execution.
- **Other services' statements to the database are normal.** `ts.config`, `ts.station`, `ts.train_type`, `ts.trip`, `ts.user`, `ts.orders` and `ts.price_config` all show the same percentiles in incident and normal periods. Only the route-service's connection is affected. This does not fit a slow statement type or a slow database, which would hit other callers too.
- **The shape is a tail in steps near 200 ms, not a steady added cost.** This is the TCP retransmission-timeout signature:
  - `SELECT ts.route_distances`: p25 0.10 → 1.91 ms, p50 0.10 → 4.52 ms, p75 → 206 ms, p90 → 378 ms, p95 → 601 ms.
  - `SELECT ts.route_stations`: p25 0.10 → 1.59 ms, p75 → 205 ms, p95 → 425 ms.
  - `SELECT ts.route`: p75 → 208 ms, p95 → 421 ms.
  - Histogram buckets for route_distances and route_stations cluster at 0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1450, 1650 and 3100 ms, with a few outliers near 13 s.
- **The route-service's own process is not saturated.** Its CPU fell (container CPU 0.057 → 0.013 cores), memory is flat, and there are no restarts. Its own Server and Internal spans have no slow time apart from the DB waits.
- **The HTTP hops are not slow.** For `ts-basic-service → ts-route-service` POST, the caller's Client span is about 1 ms longer than the callee's Server span. The time is inside the route-service, in DB waits.
- **The route-service's own span and log volume fell** (spans 8,297 → 413 per minute). Its callers mostly stopped sending traffic because the route-service was slow. That is a consequence of the fault, not a separate cause.

**Why not `database_call_slow`:** a DB-call fault is in the service's own driver. It makes particular statements slower by a steady amount and leaves the connection, the pool and other statements normal. Here the affected set includes commit and all three SELECT types on the route-service's connection, the wait comes in 200 ms steps, and the same database serves other services normally. That is the link, not the statements.

**Why `network_loss`/`network_partition` rather than `network_delay`:** delay would move the 25th, 50th and 95th percentiles together, by hundreds of ms. Here the median barely moves on most calls and the tail appears in 200 ms steps. The roughly one-third of calls that hit the tail point to heavy loss, which sits at the boundary with partition. The telemetry cannot separate those two, and the evaluator scores them the same.

**Gaps:** this case has no `hubble_*` per-connection metrics, so I could not confirm the route↔database link directly. I also did not read the text of the six route-service ERROR logs in the incident, so I have not ruled out `network_corrupt` by checking for deserialization errors. The 200 ms-step tail is consistent with loss or corruption, and I did not separate them.
